content.text: The Single Responsibility Principle doesn't say a class should do one thing. Robert C. Martin states it as "one and only one reason to change", and he is explicit that reasons to change are people: the group that asks for the change. Keep code that serves one group together, even when it does several things, and separate code that different groups care about, even when it looks related.
Payroll asks for a new rule: overtime now starts after 40 hours a week. A developer updates the

class, the pay tests pass, and the change ships. At the end of the month the operations team escalates: the hours report their auditors rely on shows different numbers, and nobody asked for that. The class was small and every method "did one thing", yet a change for one department still broke another department's work.
The belief: SRP means a class, or a method, should do only one thing. A class with
does three things, so split it; a class with a single public method follows SRP by definition.

It's easy to see where this comes from. The name invites it: "single responsibility" sounds like "one job". Martin has also long given a similar-sounding rule for functions; in a 2009 post he writes that "functions should do one thing. They should do it well. They should do it only." Same author, similar words, so the two rules blur. And many summaries, including Microsoft's architecture guide, describe SRP as objects having "only one responsibility", which reads naturally as "one task".
The half-truth: small, focused functions are good advice. It just isn't the Single Responsibility Principle, and following it doesn't prevent the bug above.
One reason to change, and reasons are people

as: each software module should have "one and only one reason to change". Then he asks the obvious question: what counts as a reason to change? Not bug fixes or refactorings; those are the programmer's job, not the program's. His answer: "This principle is about people." A module is responsible to the group that specifies its behavior. Pay rules come from finance, the audit report from operations, the database schema from the technical team. His own example uses the CFO, the COO and the CTO.
So the SRP question isn't "how many things does this class do?" It's "how many different groups could ask me to change it?"
"Do one thing" is a different rule at a different scale

The function rule is about size and readability: if you can extract a smaller, well-named function from a function, it was doing more than one thing. In that 2009 post Martin takes it as far as it goes: "Extract till you drop." You can follow it perfectly and still break SRP.
can be built from one-line methods and still answer to three departments. And a class with a dozen methods can respect SRP, as long as one group asks for all of them.
Martin offers a second wording: "Gather together the things that change for the same reasons. Separate those things that change for different reasons." He adds that this is just another way to define

. The idea is older than SOLID: Martin opens his post with David Parnas's 1972 advice to start from "design decisions which are likely to change" and design each module "to hide such a decision from the others."
When one module serves several groups, shared code becomes a channel for surprises. Martin's example: change
, and the COO starts demanding that you never change
again. In his 2020 follow-up he adds that microservices don't solve this: you can create a tangled service, or a tangled set of services, by mixing code that changes for different reasons.
The fix: split by who asks, not by verb

content.text: Finance's rule and the auditors' rule now live in two classes, each answering to one group, and they share only the
data. Saving moves to the persistence code behind

, because the schema changes for technical reasons. Both classes compute "regular hours", which looks like duplication. It isn't: a 40-hour threshold and contracted hours are different rules that happened to agree, and they will change on different days for different people. Notice what we didn't do: split
. Those pieces always change together, at finance's request, so splitting them would scatter one responsibility over three files.

SRP means one reason to change, and Martin says reasons to change are people
A class with one method follows SRP

More, smaller classes means better SRP

content.text: Open a class's recent commits or their linked tickets. If the requests come from one team, the class has one responsibility, however many methods it has. If they come from finance and from compliance, you've found two, and any helper they share is where the next surprise will come from.

blocks.title: Splitting by verb creates the opposite problem

content.text: because each "does one thing" can spread a single business rule across four files. Then one request from finance means editing four classes and hoping you found them all. SRP wants that change in one place.
How to apply it in your project
For each important class, write down who asks for changes to it: a team, a role, a regulator. One name is a good sign. Two or more makes it a candidate for a split.
Private methods or utilities called by code that serves different groups, like
, are where one group's change leaks into another group's results.
Move each group's rules into its own class or module and let them share only data. Accept that two rules may look alike for now.
Inside each class, keep extracting small, well-named functions. That's readability work, and it doesn't change who the class answers to.

items.text: SRP says a module should have one reason to change, and Martin says reasons to change are people.
"Do one thing" is a separate rule for functions; following it doesn't guarantee SRP.
Gather code that changes for the same reasons and separate code that changes for different reasons: that's cohesion and coupling.
A helper shared by two groups' code is how one team's request breaks another team's feature.
Don't split one group's rules into many tiny classes; that scatters a single responsibility.
